title: Money
hook: the love of money, not money, is the trouble (1 Timothy 6:10)
tomorrow: what does it cost to buy back an hour?

segments.voice: Yesterday, work: a gardener in Eden, and a God who stopped. Your line was work and rest. Today, what the work pays.

Two friends get their first real paychecks the same week. One says: enjoy it, it's a gift, you earned it. The other says: careful, money gets its hooks in. Both of them could open a Bible and find their verse. Christians have argued this one for a very long time: is wealth a blessing, or a danger? Today, let both sides speak.
screen: `TWO PAYCHECKS, TWO VIEWS.` → `A GIFT, OR A HOOK?` → `LET BOTH SIDES SPEAK.`

segments.voice: One side reads Proverbs: “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.” Deuteronomy tells Israel to remember that it's God who gives the power to get wealth. On this view, money is a gift. Earn it honestly, enjoy it with thanks, use it well, and don't be ashamed of it. The other side reads Mark. A rich man walks away from Jesus sad, and Jesus says: “How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!” And in Luke: “Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” Mammon is an old word for wealth, spoken of like a lord who gives orders. On this view, money is dangerous, and holding it loosely, even giving much of it away, is the safer road. Some Christians have chosen poverty on purpose for exactly this reason. Now notice where they meet. Proverbs never calls greed a blessing, and Jesus never calls coins evil. The First Letter to Timothy draws the line both can stand on: “For the love of money is the root of all evil.” The love of it. So the real question, for both sides, is who's giving the orders.
screen: `A BLESSING: IT MAKETH RICH.` · `A DANGER: HOW HARDLY.` · `GOD OR MAMMON, NOT BOTH.` · `THE LOVE OF IT IS THE ROOT.` · then, large: `MONEY IS A SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Take out a card, a bill, or your banking app, and look at it for the sit as if it were someone who works for you. Bring to mind one spending habit you repeat without thinking, and ask it plainly: are you serving something I love, or giving the orders? If you pray, you can offer the answer to God.
Money. A good servant and a demanding master; the trouble is the love of it, not the coins.
The line to keep: money is a servant, as long as the orders run one way. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your friend plans to give most of her earnings away someday, because she thinks wealth is spiritually risky. you lean the other way. what is her best case, in her own terms?

fork.reveal: her steelman is Mark and Luke: riches can become a master. yours is Proverbs: the blessing of the LORD maketh rich. both sides ask who is in charge.

notes: Day 1575 (Contentment) already made the 'love of money, not money' misquote point; so the v3 hook no longer opens on the misquote. This day's angle is the debate inside the tradition (blessing or danger), meeting at 1 Timothy 6:10 and the servant/master picture (Luke 16:13).
'Mammon is an old word for wealth' is a plain gloss, not an etymology; the lesson makes no claim about its language of origin. Confirm.
Author of 1 Timothy not named in the lesson ('the First Letter to Timothy').
Practice and fork are about noticing, not financial advice. Keep them that way.
Greek 'mamonas' (Luke 16:13, mamona) glossed 'wealth, money'. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.

v3 debate shape: two real views inside the tradition, each given its best case (Proverbs 10:22 and Deuteronomy 8:18; Mark 10:23 and Luke 16:13); the fork asks the learner to state the other side's best case. No side is ranked.
Luke 12:15 was quoted in the older draft; v3 no longer voices it, so it's kept as a paraphrase source for the trapdoor's 'a life isn't made of things' background. Consider removing.
Deuteronomy 8:18 paraphrased ('it's God who gives the power to get wealth'). Mark 10:17–22 (the rich man goes away sad) paraphrased.
'Some Christians have chosen poverty on purpose' refers to religious vows of poverty (howItsDone). Confirm wording.
'Christians have argued this one for a very long time' is a hedge, with no date or count.
